nameStory: The tree slug gets its name from its unusual habit of climbing up tree trunks and living in bark crevices, unlike most slugs that stay on the ground. This arboreal lifestyle makes it stand out among New England's slug species, which typically prefer to remain at soil level munching on garden plants.
description: The tree slug is a medium-sized land slug with a distinctive translucent, almost see-through body that lets you glimpse its internal organs. It has a notably long and narrow build compared to other slugs, rarely growing longer than about 5 inches. The most striking feature is the prominent ridge or 'keel' running down its back, which appears lighter in color against the darker organs visible through its transparent skin. This ethereal, ghost-like appearance makes it one of New England's most unusual-looking slugs.

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The body is nearly transparent like frosted glass, allowing you to see dark internal organs through the skin - a feature that immediately sets it apart from other slugs

idTips.label: Prominent back ridge
idTips.description: A sharp keel runs down the back like the ridge of a roof, appearing lighter colored against the darker organs visible beneath

idTips.label: Long narrow shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly elongated and slender compared to the broader, more rounded shape of common garden slugs

idTips.label: Tree-climbing behavior
idTips.description: Often found crawling up tree bark or hiding in bark crevices rather than on the ground like most slugs

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: Reaches up to about 5 inches long when fully extended, making it larger than many common garden slugs but not giant

habitat: Tree slugs live in wooded areas throughout New England, particularly favoring deciduous and mixed forests with mature trees that have rough, furrowed bark. They're most commonly found on tree trunks, in bark crevices, under loose bark, and around the base of large trees where they can easily access their arboreal habitat. Look for them in moist forest environments, especially after rain when they become more active.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, often seen climbing tree trunks in the evening or early morning when humidity is high. This is when they're most visible as they emerge from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid nights and after rain showers. During dry spells, they retreat deep into bark crevices and may be difficult to spot.
seasonality.fall: Still active on mild, damp days as they prepare for winter. Look for them during the day in their bark hideouts as they become less mobile.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in bark crevices or under loose bark, essentially inactive. Very rarely seen unless you carefully search bark hideouts on warmer winter days.

funFact: Tree slugs are essentially living glass animals - their bodies are so transparent that you can actually watch their internal organs working, including seeing dark food move through their digestive system like watching a biological lava lamp!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common garden slugs, but the tree slug's crystal-clear, translucent body is unmistakable once you know what to look for. Remember: if you can see through it like a window and it's on a tree, it's probably a tree slug!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tree slugs,' they're not related to sea slugs at all - they're true land snails that simply lost their shells through evolution. The scientific name was sometimes placed in the genus Limax (the common garden slugs), but their unique ecology and appearance earned them their own distinct genus.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England, the tree slug is most similar to slugs in the Limax genus (common garden slugs), but differs dramatically in its transparent body and tree-climbing lifestyle. While garden slugs are opaque and ground-dwelling, tree slugs are see-through and arboreal, making them fairly easy to distinguish once you spot one.
